etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived in the Heian period from writing the man'yōgana kanji 安 in the cursive sōsho style.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Common exclamatory sound made by people of various cultures around the world.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *a. The short form of あれ (are).
Fell into disuse in roughly the Heian period, when it was replaced by わ (wa).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ka/ → /a/
Shift in pronunciation from か (ka). Appears from the Heian period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alternative spelling of あん (an), the onbin form of あり (ari) or ある (aru), with the ん (n) omitted in writing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally a compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 早く (hayaku, “early”, adverb), from adjective 早い (hayai, “early”).
Modern Japanese -i adjectives formerly ended in -ki for the attributive form. This medial /k/ dropped out during the Muromachi period, both for the attributive form (-ki becoming -i) and for the adverbial form (-ku becoming -u). However, the adverbial form reverted back to -ku thereafter for most words, with the -u ending persisting in certain everyday set expressions, such as arigatō, ohayō, or omedetō, and in hyper-formal speech.
/ohajaku/ → /ohajau/ → /ohajoː/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 互(たが)い (tagai, “mutual relationship”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Gemination of きと (kito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Sound change of だとて (da to te), compound of だ (da, “to be”, auxiliary verb) + とて (to te, “even, also”, binding particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From もしか (moshi ka, “perhaps, if”) + したら (shitara, “if doing”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Dutch gom (“gum”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Persian قم (qom).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English marathon, from Ancient Greek Μᾰρᾰθών (Mărăthṓn).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 不(ふ) (fu-) + 自(じ)由(ゆう) (jiyū)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 世紀 (syejᴴ ki^X).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Regular development of classical 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verb 儲(まう)く (mauku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By surface analysis, 冗(じょう) (jō, “superfluous”) + 談(だん) (dan, “talk”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *maparu. Possibly related to 舞(ま)う (mau).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 地 (chi, “ground”) + 下 (ka, “under”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 妙 (MC mjiewH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 密 (MC mit).
First cited to a text from 1092.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 所 (MC srjoX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂ko₂ro₂⟩ → /tokoro/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *təkərə. Likely cognate with 床 (toko, “raised area; bed”).
A surface analysis suggests that this could be an ancient compound of ⟨to₂⟩ (Proto-Japonic *to (“place”), as in 跡 ⟨ato₂⟩, “footprint, track”, from “foot place, where one has stepped”) + ⟨ko₂⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element denoting “place”, as in ここ ⟨ko₂ko₂⟩, “here”, from “this place”) + ⟨ro₂⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element, apparently indicating within a general area, possibly as in 心 ⟨ko₂ko₂ro₂⟩, “heart, mind, emotions”, 頃 ⟨ko₂ro₂⟩, “general span of time, around a certain time”, うつろ ⟨uturo₂⟩, “hollowness, empty interior”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Listed in some sources as an abbreviation of tokoro above. However, this is also listed as cognate with 床 (toko, “raised area; bed”), which term already appears in use as far back as the Kojiki (712 CE), one of the oldest Japanese texts.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₁⟩ → /*tʷo/ → /to/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *to. Appears mainly as an affixing element indicating place, as in 後 (ato, “after; behind; the back of something”), from 跡 (ato, “footprint, track”), itself a compound of 足 (a, “foot”) + 所 (to, “place”); or in 留まる (todomaru, “to stop in a place”), itself a compound of と (to, “place”) + とまる (tomaru, “to stop”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: */toupeu/ → /touɸeu/ → /toːɸyoː/ → /toːhyoː/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare 探(さが)す (sagasu, “to search”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly related to 爪 (tsume, tsuma-, “claw”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 文 (mjun, “ornate; a kind of coin; language, literature, a letter, a character”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: A later borrowing from Middle Chinese. Compare modern Min Nan reading bûn, Hakka vûn.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Possibly a shift from an older Middle Chinese-derived reading pun. Earlier Japanese writing was ambiguous regarding the final n sound spelled ん in modern Japanese, with this sound often spelled (and possibly pronounced) as む (mu) instead.
*/pumu/ → /pumi/ → /ɸumi/
This reading appears in the Heian period, in works such as The Tale of Genji.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Uncertain. Appears in texts from the early Heian period. Compare Miyako あやぐ (ayagu), あーぐ (āgu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from earlier yeda, from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yonta. Cognate with Kunigami 枝 (yudā), Miyako 枝 (yuda), Okinawan 枝 (yida), 枝 (yuda), Yaeyama 枝 (yuda), Yonaguni 枝 (duda). The vowel change is irregular.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 植え (ue, “planting”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 植える ueru “to plant (a seed, a plant)”) + 木 (ki, “tree or shrub”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/idumi/ → /id͡zumi/ → (for most modern Japanese dialects; see also Yotsugana) /izumi/
From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
Compound of 出づ (ancient reading idu, modern izu, “to come out”) + 水 (mi, “water”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 灯 (“light”) + 油 (“oil”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨tutuku⟩ → /t͡sut͡suku/ → /t͡sud͡zuku/ → /t͡suzuku/
From Old Japanese 續く (tutuku), with the shift to voicing of the second tsu developing around the Middle Japanese stage.
Cognate with 綴(つづ)る (tsuzuru, “to spell, to write”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pada/ → /ɸada/ → /hada/.
From Old Japanese, Proto-Japonic *panta. First attested in the Man'yōshū, completed sometime around 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Modern form of Old Japanese adjective よし (yoshi).
/joɕi/ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → /joki/ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /joi/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phonetic shift from the Old Japanese yoshi form of yoi above. Already in use as early as the Nihon Shoki, circa 720, then becoming common in eastern Japanese from the Edo period. This form is now obsolete, though it may still be found in some dialects.
/joɕi/ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → /eɕi/ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → /eki/ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /ei/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phonetic shift from ei above. This is now the most common form used in casual spoken Japanese.
/ei/ → /ii/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/musi/ → /muɕi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mosi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 面 (MC mjienH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Proto-Japonic *tura (“face”).
Cognate with Okinawan ちら.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By apheresis from おも (omo, “face”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 順 (jun, “favorable”) + 調 (chō, “tone”).
